Senses.Explanation: A later label for four statements recorded in Linji's own late-evening address: at times he takes away the person but not the surroundings; at times the surroundings but not the person; at times both person and surroundings; and at times neither person nor surroundings. In Linji's record each member is followed by a monk's question and Linji's answer. For example, the first is answered with the warm sun spreading brocade over the ground, while the fourth is answered with a king ascending the jeweled hall and a rustic elder singing. The label itself does not occur in Linji's own record. The Eye of Humans and Gods later lists it beside the Three Mysteries, Three Essentials, Four Host-and-Guest Positions, and Diamond-King Treasure Sword. That compilation also grades the four: for a person of middle-lower capacity it gives taking away the surroundings but not the teaching; for middle-upper capacity, taking away surroundings and teaching but not the person, with a variant reading that takes away the teaching but not the surroundings; for one below the highest capacity, taking away both person and surroundings; and for a person beyond rank, taking away neither. This later wording uses person, teaching, and surroundings where Linji's recorded set uses person and surroundings. Nanyuan later tests Fengxue by asking, 'The Four Selections—what teaching do they select?' Fengxue answers, 'Ordinary words do not stick in ordinary feelings; they have already fallen into holy understanding.' Later records also use each member as a test question, borrow the label for the National Teacher Shao's separate set, and explicitly call a requested public case 'the Four Selections.'
Senses.Note: Current Zen-scoped counts are 121 matches in 75 files for the principal spelling and 35 in 21 files for the variant spelling. The four statements are Linji's; the collective label and student-capacity grading are later. The late-evening address and informal-convocation witnesses belong to Linji's record, while the Eye of Humans and Gods catalogue and the Nanyuan–Fengxue examination are compiled or raised material. Do not read the compilation's person/teaching/surroundings wording back into Linji's person/surroundings set, and do not attribute the National Teacher Shao's separate fourfold set to Linji.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the Four Modes of Illumination and Function
AlternateTargets: Linji's four modes of illumination and function
Senses.Explanation: A four-member set recorded in Linji's sayings: first illuminate, then function; first function, then illuminate; illuminate and function simultaneously; and illuminate and function at different times. Linji states that he sometimes uses each mode. His following gloss says that in first-illuminate-then-function a person is present; in first-function-then-illuminate a teaching is present; simultaneous illumination and function drive away the plowman's ox, take the hungry person's food, strike the bone for marrow, and painfully apply needle and awl; illumination and function at different times have question and answer. The Eye of Humans and Gods preserves the labeled set and later comments. Shoushan turns its members into direct questions. Fenyang says that every phrase must contain the Three Mysteries and have illumination and function, whether illumination comes first, function comes first, both are simultaneous, or they occur at different times. Langye compares the first with showing a lion's claws and teeth, the second with releasing an elephant king's power, the simultaneous mode with a dragon obtaining water and making rain and clouds, and the different-time mode with guiding an infant and caring for a child. A compact compendium repeats Linji's person, teaching, driving-away-and-taking-food, and question-and-answer glosses. A later master maps the four onto four staff actions: holding the staff crosswise, raising it upright, turning it upside down, and striking it down once. Later lists place the set beside the Three Mysteries and Essentials, Four Selections, Four Host-and-Guest Positions, and Four Shouts. The corpus has 31 label matches in 22 files; the four member phrases circulate much more widely.
Senses.Note: Linji's full fourfold statement is valid main text in the Collection of Ancient Worthies, in his address to the assembly. In the Taisho edition of Linji's record, the same passage survives only in an apparatus note from another edition and is therefore excluded as main-text evidence; the running text has only the statement that illumination and function are simultaneous and originally have no before or after. The Eye of Humans and Gods and Compendium of the Five Lamps are compiled presentations. Shoushan, Fenyang, Langye, and Fojian Huiqin supply later questions, comparisons, and staff deployments; none of those later words is attributed to Linji. Current counts: Four Modes of Illumination and Function 31/22 files; first illuminate then function 191/75; first function then illuminate 185/74; simultaneous illumination and function 320/116; illumination and function at different times 188/74.

Senses.Explanation: The components mean “four” (四), “guest” (賓), and “host” (主): "the four guest-host [configurations]." In the corpus it names the four ways a teacher (主/host, 善知識) and a student (賓/guest, 學人) meet, one of the numbered device-sets of the Linji (臨濟) house. STRUCTURAL FACT: the compound (四賓主) does NOT occur in the primary (臨濟錄) (T47n1985, 0 occurrences of the compound, main text and apparatus alike); there Linji names the four in prose within his long (示眾), on teacher and student meeting (如主客相見便有言論往來) — (喚作客看主) (called guest-sees-host), (此是主看客) (this is host-sees-guest), (此喚作主看主) (this is called host-sees-host), (呼為客看客) (termed guest-sees-guest). So reads the Taisho main text, with (客) for the guest; the Ming-edition variant carried in the Taisho apparatus gives the passage with (賓) (喚作賓看主…主看賓…賓看賓), the graph used by the later tradition. The numbered label and the phrase-name (四賓主) are a later systematization, set out in (人天眼目) (T48n2006), under the head (臨濟門庭), with an explicit (四賓主者)…(也) definition keyed to "nostrils" (鼻孔): (師家有鼻孔)。(名主中主)。(學人有鼻孔)。(名賓中主)。(師家無鼻孔)。(名主中賓)。(學人無鼻孔)。(名賓中賓)。(與曹洞賓主不同). The corpus carries two enumeration schemes for the four — the (看)-scheme (客看主・主看客・主看主・客看客 in the Taisho 臨濟錄 main text; 賓看主・主看賓・主看主・賓看賓 in its Ming-edition variant and in later texts, e.g. X73n1457 有時賓看主，有時主看主，有時賓看賓) and the (中)-scheme (主中主)・(賓中主)・(主中賓)・(賓中賓) (人天眼目). The set is grouped with Linji's other numbered devices (三玄三要、四料揀、四照用、四喝): (昔臨濟大師建立四料揀)、(四賓主)、(四照用)、(三玄)、(三要). CONTRAST the texts themselves draw: Linji's (四賓主) vs. Caodong's — (人天眼目) states (與曹洞賓主不同) and, of the Caodong set, (四賓主)。(不同臨濟)。(主中賓)。(體中用也). The texts enumerate and name the four and distinguish Linji's from Caodong's; beyond the attested (有鼻孔)/(無鼻孔) glosses they add no further reading, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Describe-only structural facts: (1) the compound (四賓主) is a lamp/eye-of-humans-and-gods systematization of the guest-host prose in Linji's own record — the primary (臨濟錄) (T47n1985) names the four configurations but not the numbered set. (2) There are TWO distinct (四賓主) systems in the corpus — Linji's and Caodong's (曹洞) — the texts explicitly flag them as (不同) (與曹洞賓主不同 / 不同臨濟); do not conflate them. (3) Two co-existing enumerations of Linji's four: the (看)-scheme (X看Y; with 客 in the Taisho 臨濟錄 main text, 賓 in its Ming-edition variant and later texts) and the (中)-scheme (X中Y). Nested/related: (賓主) (t_6da91f8ce284) is the shorter constituent (a genuine constituent relation). Attribution: the (人天眼目) exposition and the enumerations are compiler/discourse material without a single-speaker head → MasterName null; only the primary (臨濟錄) (示眾) is attributed to (臨濟義玄).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "swap out the eyes" (換卻眼睛). In ordinary wording this would name a bodily exchange; Chan records use it as an accusation that a saying, written formulation, sight, sound, or teacher has displaced a person's own seeing. A commentary says a monk asking Xuansha about his own self had his eyes swapped out by Xuansha's reply. Shiyu says altered wording and changed characters (改文易字) swap out people's eyes, and elsewhere says waterbirds, groves, bells, and gongs do it. Sanyi warns against letting the writing brush exchange black beans for one's eyes (毛錐子將黑荳換卻眼睛), then identifies bird-script, dragon-writing, paper, ink, and written characters as fit for ordinary circulation rather than Chan discussion. A case comment even judges the words "Where is the eminent monk?" (高僧何在) themselves to have plainly swapped out the eyes. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore an adversarial verdict about seeing being commandeered; the texts apply it to both words and sensory displays, not to literal surgery.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 63 hits in 45 allowlisted texts, concentrated in later discourse records and case comments. Attested agents include a master's reply, rewritten words, landscape, sounds, written characters, and a case question. No in-corpus occurrence defines a physical operation.
